claims.claim: Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units in a narrow way.
The narrow approach should include stronger limits on increases inside tenancies, tenure security, and better enforcement.
A hard cap on initial rents should not be imposed.
Tenants in subdivided units pay a 15 to 25 percent premium per square foot compared with ordinary flats.
The rent burden for subdivided unit households rose from 31 to 34 percent of income.
Many subdivided unit tenants are new arrivals or families waiting for public housing, so the unit is not a real choice.
A 10 percent cap-induced rent reduction removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of SDU-type stock over five years.
In a market of about 111,200 units, this means thousands of units lost.
A 15 percent initial-rent cut predicts a net transfer of about 900 dollars per month to incumbents, at the cost of 3,000 to 4,000 households per year unable to enter the segment, mostly new arrivals.
This is a transfer from those outside to those already inside.
When Berlin capped rents on about 1.5 million flats in 2020, listing supply contracted within a year as owners withheld or rerouted flats.
When the Berlin law was struck down in 2021, rents for new contracts jumped above the pre-cap trend.
Caps bind differently on new entrants than incumbents, and the bill is handed to those still outside.
The 2021 ordinance capped increases within existing tenancies but left initial rents unregulated.
Mrs Wong, who has lived in her unit for nine years without a written agreement, says the ordinance changed nothing she can see.
A better approach combines tenure security and a light rent band.
The NGO report finds that 61 percent of tenants would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year security.
Mr Chan was given two weeks notice after asking for a repair.
A legal opinion says a band set by a published, indexed per-square-foot rate could be defended as rate-capping rather than confiscation.
New York's light scheme has shown modest stock contraction.
Inspection capacity covers under 6 percent of stock a year, and a band needs a tenancy register estimated at 40 to 60 staff-years.
Tenure security should come first and the band only after enforcement capacity is built.
Mrs Wong supports a hard cap and thinks landlords would not leave.
The evidence on lost units and blocked newcomers makes a hard cap risky for the same people Mrs Wong speaks for.
The landlords' exit threat is weak because they admit having no margin data.
